result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.find_maximal_independent_sets()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find multiple distinct maximal independent sets. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L35213-L35315){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.find_maximal_independent_sets( count=10, seed=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Find maximal independent sets](/assets/graphs/find-maximal-independent-sets.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Left: a five-node graph, a triangle 2, 3, 5 with pendant nodes 1 and 4. Right: three miniature copies, each highlighting one maximal independent set in the accent color, listed beside it: [1, 3], [1, 4, 5], and [2, 4]." width="100%"} Runs the randomized `maximal_independent_set()` algorithm repeatedly, each time with a different random node order, and keeps every result that hasn't been seen before. A graph usually has many maximal independent sets of different sizes, and a single call returns just one of them; sampling several lets you explore the alternatives. This is useful for: - approximating a *maximum* independent set by keeping the largest of many candidates - finding alternative conflict-free batches (for example, different sets of jobs that can run together) and choosing among them by some other criterion - ensemble methods or robustness checks that need several distinct solutions At most `3 * count` attempts are made. Duplicate sets are discarded, so the method stops early once `count` distinct sets are found and returns fewer than `count` sets if the attempts run out first (for example, when the graph only has a few maximal independent sets). Like `maximal_independent_set()`, it ignores edge direction. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [count]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[10]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Number of distinct maximal independent sets to return. Default is `10`. Fewer sets are returned if not enough distinct ones turn up within `3 * count` attempts. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Base random seed for reproducibility. When given, attempt `i` (counting from `0`) uses seed `seed + i`, so the same `seed=` always returns the same list of sets. If `None` (the default), every attempt draws its order from system entropy and results vary between calls. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[list[int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of distinct maximal independent sets, in the order they were found. Each set is a list of node IDs sorted in ascending order. May contain fewer than `count` sets. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Runs `maximal_independent_set()` up to $3 \cdot \text{count}$ times with distinct seeds derived from a common base, giving $O(\text{count} \cdot (V + E))$ total work. Duplicate results are dropped, so the returned list may be shorter than `count` when the graph's independent structure is tight enough that different starting orders keep converging to the same set. Sampling a diverse pool this way is the usual bridge between the fast-but-maximal single call and the slow-but-maximum exact solver: keeping the largest set out of several attempts often approaches the true maximum on real-world graphs. ## Examples {.doc-examples} An 8-node cycle has many maximal independent sets. Sampling with a fixed seed returns several distinct ones, with sizes 3 or 4: ::: {#45300630 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_cycle_graph(8) sets = graph.find_maximal_independent_sets(count=5, seed=23) # Each entry is a distinct maximal independent set sets ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [[1, 4, 6], [1, 4, 7], [2, 5, 8], [3, 6, 8], [2, 4, 6, 8]] ``` ::: ::: Since maximal doesn't mean maximum, generating several candidates and keeping the largest is a simple way to approximate the true maximum independent set. Comparing the smallest and largest candidates shows how much the size can vary: ::: {#acbfb414 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_gnm_graph(n=50, m=100, seed=23) sets = graph.find_maximal_independent_sets(count=20, seed=0) best = max(sets, key=len) # (smallest candidate, largest candidate) (min(len(s) for s in sets), len(best)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (17, 24) ``` ::: ::: In a complete graph, every node conflicts with every other, so each maximal independent set is a single node. There are only 8 such sets, so asking for 10 returns just 8: ::: {#ebd62adb .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_full_graph(8) sets = graph.find_maximal_independent_sets(count=10, seed=1) # (number of sets found, distinct set sizes) (len(sets), {len(s) for s in sets}) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (8, {1}) ``` ::: :::
